item.research_question: What alloying and scaling conditions lead to the strongest both ductile and stable materials?
item.material_system: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) thin films and pillars
item.processing_route: d.c. magnetron co-sputtering on (100) silicon or sapphire substrates at room temperature; Ion beam-assisted deposition (IBAD) used with 1.2 keV beam energy, 5 mA current, and 35° incidence angle to reduce grain size; Focused Ga ion beams (FIB) used to mill pillars with diameters of ~1 μm, 500, 200, and 100 nm
item.test_conditions: Microcompression tests at a strain rate of 2 × 10−3 s−1; Thermal annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days in argon atmosphere
key_findings: HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ~10 GPa, one order of magnitude higher than the bulk form.
Compressive plastic strains over 30% were achieved in smaller pillars without cracking.
580-nm Normal HEA pillars show a yield strength of ~5 GPa, while 580-nm IBAD HEA pillars reach ~6.5 GPa.
Smallest IBAD HEA pillars (~70–100 nm diameter) exhibit yield strengths of ~8–10 GPa.
After annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days, HEA pillars retain a high yield strength of ~5 GPa, whereas pure W films show significant grain growth and pore formation.
IBAD HEA pillars exhibit a log–log slope of −0.2 for the relationship between flow stress and pillar diameter, indicating the lowest size dependence among reported pillars.
item.mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is attributed to the simultaneous operation of four strengthening mechanisms: lattice friction, Taylor hardening, source-controlled strength, and grain-boundary strengthening. The excellent thermal stability is attributed to relatively low grain-boundary energy due to the highly disordered grain interiors in HEAs, which lowers the driving force for grain-boundary migration compared to pure metals.
item.limitations: The text notes that large pillars (>1 μm) experience cracking at strains larger than ~20% and that the smallest pillars (~70–100 nm) show higher scattering levels in strength due to inhomogeneous distribution of grain boundaries.
item.future_work: The authors state that mechanical tests for small-scale HEAs at high temperatures are still needed to prove their capability as high-temperature materials, and that further work is required to optimize small-scale HEAs for applications, such as determining the best alloying elements and optimized grain and specimen size combinations.
quotes: Here we report a strategy for the fabrication of refractory HEA thin films and small-sized pillars that consist of strongly textured, columnar and nanometre-sized grains.

Such HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ∼10 GPa—among the highest reported strengths in micro-/nano-pillar compression and one order of magnitude higher than that of its bulk form.
The excellent thermal stability of the nanocrystalline HEA film could be attributed to their relatively low grain-boundary energy.
